title: How Ears Hear
objective: After this level you can explain how the ear turns sound waves into signals.
summary: The eardrum vibrates, three tiny bones amplify, and the fluid-filled cochlea's hair cells, sorted by pitch, send signals to the brain. Human hair cells never grow back.

cards.headline: Every sound you hear ends as a ripple in a snail-shaped tube of fluid.
cards.body: A voice, a song, a dog barking: each arrives as sound waves in the air. Your ear's job is to turn them into electrical signals your brain can read. It takes a relay from air to bone to liquid.

cards.headline: Drum, bones, fluid
cards.body: Sound waves travel down your ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates. It hands the vibrations to three tiny bones in the middle ear: the malleus, the incus and the stapes, a stirrup-shaped bone that is the smallest of the three. The bones amplify the vibrations and pass them into the cochlea, a snail-shaped, fluid-filled structure in the inner ear. Air, then bone, then liquid.

cards.headline: Hair cells ride the wave
cards.body: Inside the cochlea, the vibrations start a traveling wave along a membrane, and sensory hair cells ride it. Cells near the wide end respond to high pitches, like a baby crying; those toward the center respond to low ones, like a big dog barking. As the cells move, tiny bristles on top bend, channels open and an electrical signal is born. The auditory nerve carries it to your brain.

cards.fact: Your hair cells are not on the replacement list.
cards.context: Unlike the hair cells of birds and amphibians, human hair cells don't grow back, and their damage and death cause most noise-induced hearing loss. Compare Level 10, where about 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day. The ones you hear with have to last.

questions.prompt: What are the malleus, the incus and the stapes?

options.label: Three parts of the cochlea's membrane
options.rationale: The cochlea is in the inner ear, past the bones.

options.label: Three tiny bones in the middle ear
Three nerves leading to the brain
options.rationale: The auditory nerve carries the signal.

options.label: Three layers of the eardrum
options.rationale: The eardrum passes vibrations to them.

questions.explanation: The malleus, incus and stapes are the middle ear's three tiny bones; they amplify the eardrum's vibrations and pass them to the cochlea.

questions.prompt: How can your cochlea tell a baby's cry from a big dog's bark?

options.label: The eardrum sorts the sounds before the cochlea gets them
options.rationale: The eardrum just vibrates and passes it on.

options.label: One single hair cell hears every sound, one at a time
options.rationale: Many hair cells ride the wave.

options.label: Hair cells in different places respond to different pitches
Low sounds skip the cochlea and go straight to the nerve

questions.explanation: Hair cells near the cochlea's wide end respond to high pitches and those toward the center to low pitches.

questions.prompt: Level 10 said about 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day. What happens to your hearing's hair cells?

options.label: Once they die, they don't grow back
They regrow, as they do in birds
options.rationale: Birds' hair cells regrow; ours don't.

options.label: They are rebuilt from blood cells
options.rationale: Blood cells lead the daily turnover, but don't become hair cells.

questions.explanation: Most of your cells are renewed, but human hair cells don't grow back once they die, unlike those of birds and amphibians.
